description: We are a solo student-led team passionate about Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Computer Vision, and space technology. Our goal is to transform NASA's NISAR satellite radar data into meaningful, interactive insights that help identify and understand changes occurring on Earth's surface. We aim to combine geospatial analysis, image processing, and accessible visualisation to make complex Earth observation data easier to interpret.
summary: TerraScope AI is a dashboard that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar (HH and HV polarizations) to map possible surface water and possible flood-related water change over Delhi and Dehradun, India. Radar sees through monsoon clouds, when optical satellites are blind. Our pipeline streams only a 20 km city window from each multi-gigabyte NISAR GCOV file, learns a water threshold from the image itself, and compares two dates of the same orbit track. It checks its own evidence: when two images are not comparable, it withholds change results instead of reporting artefacts. This check detected that one NISAR image (5 September 2026) is degraded over our Delhi window, so that image was excluded. TerraScope shows what radar can and cannot tell us, making satellite flood monitoring transparent and reproducible on an ordinary student laptop.
details:
What it does. TerraScope AI maps possible surface water on two NISAR radar dates and classifies the change between them into four classes: no significant water change, persistent possible water, newly detected possible water, and decreased possible water. A Streamlit dashboard shows HH and HV radar images, water maps, a change map on an OpenStreetMap base, statistics, warnings and a plain-language explanation for Delhi and Dehradun, India.

How it works.

1. Data access: NASA's earthaccess library finds NISAR L2 GCOV granules and streams only a 20 km x 20 km window around each city (about 16 MB per layer instead of 6-7 GB per file), so it runs on an 8 GB laptop.

2. Valid pixels: a pixel is used only if it has data on both dates, in both polarizations, and inside the NISAR validity mask.

3. Speckle reduction: a 5 x 5 averaging filter in linear power, then conversion to decibels.

4. Split-based thresholding: the window is cut into tiles (2 km, 1 km or 500 m). Only tiles that clearly contain both water and land teach the water threshold (Otsu's method per tile, Ashman's D of at least 3). HH and HV each get one threshold shared by both dates. If too few tiles qualify, the result is flagged low confidence instead of guessed.

5. Change classification: new or decreased water also needs a backscatter change of at least 3 dB; patches smaller than 3 x 3 pixels are removed as noise.

6. Quality gates: if the two dates correlate below 0.70 (100 m blocks), change results are withheld. The scene-wide shift between dates and a +/-1 dB threshold-sensitivity test are reported.

Results (real NISAR data).

- Dehradun, 29 Aug to 10 Sep 2026 (track 055): the two images are comparable (correlation 0.97 HH / 0.98 HV). No radar-detectable open water on either date and no detected water change within the 20 km window.

- Delhi: track 055 does not image Delhi, so we used track 156. Our quality gate found that the 5 Sep 2026 image is degraded over Delhi (correlation 0.48 / 0.57; dark surfaces brightened by 8-10 dB, bright surfaces darkened by 2-11 dB, surface detail lost), so change results were withheld automatically instead of reporting false water loss. The 24 Aug 2026 image gives a single-date map of about 12.5 km2 of possible water along the Yamuna (HV threshold -18.6 dB learned from the image; 9.4-16.8 km2 if the threshold moves by 1 dB). A replacement pair, 24 Aug to 17 Sep 2026, has been configured; its result is not included here.

We do not claim that a flood did or did not happen, and we claim no accuracy figure: no reference flood data was used.

Why it matters. Monsoon floods happen under clouds, and L-band radar sees through cloud day and night. TerraScope shows how open NISAR data can become a transparent first-look water map on ordinary hardware, and how to check whether a result deserves trust before anyone acts on it.

What makes it creative. Instead of always producing a map, the pipeline tests its own evidence: it learns thresholds only where water and land are both present, measures how sensitive the result is, and refuses to report change when the two images do not show the same scene.

Tools. Python; earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, Shapely, rasterio (GDAL), Matplotlib, Pillow, Streamlit, folium, pytest; GDAL command-line tools (OSGeo4W). Tested with 37 unit tests on synthetic data plus end-to-end tests.

Limitations. Both dates are inside the monsoon, so there is no dry-season baseline. Radar shadow in hills and smooth urban surfaces can look like water. The product has no layover/shadow mask. No ground-truth validation yet.

Method references. Otsu (1979), IEEE Trans. Systems, Man, and Cybernetics; Martinis, Twele and Voigt (2009), Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences; Chini et al. (2017), IEEE Trans. Geoscience and Remote Sensing; Ashman, Bird and Zepf (1994), The Astronomical Journal.
